title: Why “Black Mass” Is Critical
key_claim: China controls 75 percent of global capacity for black mass recycling and leads across every recovery technology while the EU lags in both technology and capacity; by 2035 an estimated 15 percent of global critical-mineral supply will come from recycling black mass, more than double the current 7 percent, and 73 percent of global black mass will come from end-of-life batteries (up from 20 percent in 2024); the EU Critical Raw Materials Act mandates that 25 percent of consumption come from domestic recycling and caps any single supplier at 65 percent; the EU has classified black mass as hazardous waste and is restricting exports from 2026 but lacks the infrastructure to meet 2026-2027 deadlines, so if it bans black mass exports the material will simply be stockpiled; the DRC's February 2025 suspension of cobalt exports triggered a sharp rise in cobalt and black mass prices, illustrating how primary and secondary sources are now linked.
frame_summary: DGAP argues that battery recycling and black mass are the next arena of geopolitical competition over critical minerals, and that Europe risks trading its dependence on Chinese primary supply for a new dependence on Chinese secondary (recycling) supply unless it builds sovereign capacity rather than relying on joint ventures.
notes: Structural anchor: canonical framing source (DGAP Policy Brief No. 4, 23 Feb 2026, Yuka Kobayashi). 3-6m band. Rich quantification and the stockpiling argument.

publisher: The State Council of the People's Republic of China (english.www.gov.cn)
title: China to strengthen recycling management of used power batteries from NEVs
key_claim: China's MIIT and five other departments jointly issued interim measures for the recycling and comprehensive utilization of used new energy vehicle (NEV) power batteries, taking effect on April 1, 2026, assigning each NEV battery a digital identity and establishing a national full-lifecycle traceability information platform; in 2025 China's NEV production and sales both exceeded 16 million units, over half of domestic new vehicle sales, and industry experts project that used-battery generation will exceed 1 million tonnes by 2030.
frame_summary: The Chinese government frames the interim measures as a full-lifecycle, full-chain formalisation of its battery-recycling sector, positioning China to capture and process the coming wave of retired NEV batteries through mandatory traceability and producer responsibility.
notes: Tier 1 primary (Chinese State Council English portal, Xinhua). Published 16 Jan 2026 (179 days before cycle date, inside the 180-day audit window); DGAP is the flagged structural anchor. Primary source for the 1 April 2026 MIIT framework.

title: Out of the Dependency Trap: Why Germany's and Europe's Critical Raw Materials Policy Falls Short and How to Fix It
date_evidence: 12 May 2026 (byline under authors Florian Klumpp, Jakob Hensing, Thorsten Benner, Louca Derville)
key_claim: GPPi argues that Germany and the EU remain heavily dependent on China for critical raw materials and that their policy is too supply-side, wrongly assuming that improving conditions for private projects will drive diversification against China's state-backed, vertically integrated dominance; among four levers (stockpiling, primary supply, recycling, demand reduction), recycling and substitution remain underutilised as resilience tools, and accelerating them requires specific collection and recovery obligations to keep materials in dedicated value chains, tighter control of scrap exports alongside better intra-EU waste flows, and market-shaping demand and price interventions rather than framework conditions alone.
frame_summary: GPPi argues that Europe must shift from a supply-side, framework-conditions approach to an active market-shaping strategy - including tighter scrap-export control and demand-and-price interventions - because captured market structures, not geology, are the binding constraint on breaking dependence on China.
notes: Tier 2 think tank, within window. Supports the market-shaping and scrap-export-control thread.

title: Chinese recycling crackdown reshapes black mass flows, pressures recycled cobalt market
key_claim: China's nationwide battery-recycling framework, effective April 1, 2026, is prompting informal shredding operators to liquidate black mass and is releasing lower-cost recycled cobalt into the market: NCM black mass payables fell to 74-75% DDP China (week ending 11 June 2026), and scrap-fed cobalt sulfate was offered at 84,000-85,000 yuan per tonne (some lots as low as 81,000) against 91,000-93,000 yuan for primary hydroxide-based material, displacing primary feedstock from spot activity; China processed more than 400,000 tonnes of spent power batteries in 2025 (up around 33% year on year, per CATARC), yet licensed recyclers run at just 20-30% utilisation, and by 2030 more than 2.8 million NEVs are expected to reach end of life with retirements exceeding 1 million tonnes, even as the DRC's cobalt export suspension constrains primary hydroxide supply.
frame_summary: Fastmarkets reports that China's formalisation of its battery-recycling sector is, in the near term, flushing cheap recycled cobalt into the market and resetting the price floor, while confirming China's scale advantage in retired-battery feedstock and licensed refining capacity.
notes: Tier 2 price reporting agency, within window. Primary source for the black-mass payable and cobalt-sulfate price data and the April 1 framework's market effect.

title: One Year After China Reopened Black Mass Imports: What's Really Changed?
key_claim: Nearly a year after China reopened qualified black mass imports in August 2025, China's position as the world's largest battery-recycling and hydrometallurgical processing market has made overseas black mass an increasingly important feedstock, and Malaysian black mass transactions have shifted toward referencing China's ternary (three-metal) payable system, so domestic Chinese pricing has become an important benchmark for part of the overseas market; a water-soluble fluorine specification still constrains direct imports, prompting an emerging model in which black mass is converted to intermediate products such as mixed nickel-cobalt carbonate overseas before high-value refining is completed in China.
frame_summary: SMM argues that China's reopening of black mass imports has deepened the linkage between overseas and Chinese recycling markets, extending China's pricing and refining gravity across borders even where direct imports are constrained.
notes: Tier 3 specialist trade analysis, within window. Supports the cross-border enclosure thread (China's pricing gravity, overseas intermediate processing).

title: Congo cobalt exporters fear losing quotas due to administrative glitch, sources say
key_claim: The Democratic Republic of Congo's strategic-minerals regulator ARECOMS operates an export-quota regime for cobalt, and an administrative failure to notify customs from July 1 2026 left major producers including CMOC, Glencore, ERG and Huayou unable to complete export declarations; industry sources estimate 60-75% of companies were unlikely to meet the quota-utilisation deadline, putting up to 20,000 tonnes of cobalt exports, worth approximately US$1.1 billion, at risk.
frame_summary: The report shows the DRC actively administering cobalt supply through export quotas, keeping primary cobalt tight and reinforcing the link between constrained primary supply and the rising role of recycled, black-mass-derived cobalt.
notes: Tier 3 (SMM relaying Reuters). Within window. Directional corroboration of the DRC cobalt-quota constraint that interacts with the recycled-cobalt price floor.

title: China Battery Recycling Regulation: Black Mass & Cobalt Sulphate Prices 2026
key_claim: China's April 1 2026 recycling framework upgrades recovery targets to at least 90% for lithium (from 85%) and at least 98% for nickel, cobalt and manganese (leading operators reporting 99.6%), mandates a national digital battery ID (GB/T 34014) and full producer responsibility, and removes cascade utilisation as a separate tier, standards that already exceed the EU Battery Regulation's targets of at least 80% lithium and at least 95% nickel/cobalt/manganese recovery by 2031 and its battery passport mandate scheduled for 2027; the near-term flood of recycled cobalt is partly one-off informal-sector liquidation, but China's structural battery-retirement growth makes recycled cobalt a permanent and scalable share of supply.
frame_summary: Discovery Alert argues that China's recycling formalisation is creating short-term price dislocation but a durable, scalable recycled-metal supply base, and that its recovery-rate and traceability standards now lead global benchmarks.
notes: Tier 4 investor-facing aggregator, within window; used for directional corroboration of China vs EU recovery-target comparison and the structural-vs-transitional framing. Draws on Fastmarkets and CATARC data.
